title.narrative: Emergency Humanitarian Response to the Northern Afghanistan Earthquake

description.narrative: Key vulnerable groups include: (1) Female-headed households (targeting 300, or 40% of MPCA beneficiaries), who face elevated GBV risks, economic exclusion, and shelter instability per UNFPA assessments (November 2025); (2) Households with persons with disabilities (250 targeted, 33% of total), including mobility-impaired elderly requiring adaptive hygiene items and heating; (3) Elderly-led or child-headed families (200 targeted, 27%), shielding against hypothermia and trauma as winter intensifies; and (4) Pregnant/lactating women and children under five (integrated across 60% of PSS reach, 1,170 individuals), addressing nutrition and psychosocial gaps amid overcrowded conditions. These groups, comprising over 70% of overall beneficiaries, align with the Alert's call to prioritize unassisted, high-risk populations to avert secondary crises like disease outbreaks and displacement.

On 3 November 2025, a 6.3 magnitude earthquake struck northern Afghanistan, impacting Baghlan, Balkh, Jawzjan, Kunduz, Samangan, and Sar-e-Pul provinces. The disaster caused severe damage to homes, public infrastructure, and essential services, leading to casualties and widespread displacement. Preliminary assessments report 26 deaths, 1,172 injuries, and 3,027 affected families (approximately 21,189 individuals). Around 874 homes were destroyed and 2,153 were damaged, alongside losses of food stocks, livestock, and agricultural assets, further undermining livelihoods and food security. The earthquake exacerbates existing vulnerabilities amid economic hardship and limited access to basic services. As winter approaches, affected families face heightened risks of inadequate shelter, exposure to cold, health outbreaks (respiratory and waterborne diseases), and food insecurity. Damaged infrastructure and restricted access to remote areas continue to challenge response efforts. Vulnerable groups, women, children, and the elderly, are at increased risk due to poor shelter and limited healthcare. Humanitarian partners are mobilizing to provide emergency shelter, food assistance, health services, and WASH support to address immediate needs.

The proposed project, led by Cordaid in partnership with OHW, aims to deliver an integrated and life-saving humanitarian response to communities affected by the recent earthquake in Balkh and Samangan provinces. The earthquake of 3 November 2025 caused significant destruction to homes and community infrastructure, disrupted essential services, and severely impacted the livelihoods of already vulnerable populations. The situation has been further exacerbated by the approaching winter, leaving many families without adequate shelter, heating, or basic household necessities. In response to these urgent needs, the project will implement a multi-sectoral and cash-based intervention that addresses the most critical humanitarian priorities identified through rapid needs assessments and coordination with the Afghanistan National Disaster Management Authority (ANDMA), the Disaster Response Committees of the Department of Refugees and Repatriation (DoRR), and relevant humanitarian clusters, including Emergency Shelter/Non-Food Items (ES/NFI), Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), and Protection. The intervention will target earthquake-affected households in Sholgara, Marmul, and Kishendeh districts of Balkh Province, as well as Hazrat-e-Sultan, Aybak, and Feroz Nakhchir districts of Samangan Province. The project will provide Multi-Purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA) to 750 of the most vulnerable women-headed and child-headed households, enabling them to meet their immediate needs such as food, healthcare, and essential household items. Additionally, 750 families will receive cash for heating, in line with the ES/NFI Cluster’s standard winterization package, to help them purchase fuel and heating materials to protect against the harsh winter conditions. To address health and sanitation concerns in temporary and overcrowded living conditions, the project will provide hygiene promotion sessions to 1,750 families and distribute hygiene kits to 1,000 households, ensuring access to essential hygiene items and improved awareness of disease prevention practices. Furthermore, psychosocial support (PSS) and referral services will be provided by dedicated project psychosocial couselors to 1,750 individuals and families experiencing trauma and stress related to the earthquake, helping them regain emotional well-being and access specialized services where needed as per assessment, there are already specialized medical and child protection centers whom they will be meaningfully referred, additionly will refresh service mapping for extensive support services available. This integrated response was designed based on rapid needs assessments conducted by Partner 1 field teams between 5–9 November 2025, which identified cash, heating, hygiene, and psychosocial support as the most urgent priorities. Consultations with affected communities, including women’s groups, elders, and youth representatives, confirmed that cash-based interventions are the most effective and dignified means of addressing immediate needs, while winterization support is critical to prevent loss of life due to extreme cold. Community feedback also highlighted the growing need for psychosocial support to address the emotional distress caused by loss, displacement, and uncertainty.

title.narrative: CSH-R1: Number of people benefitting from unconditional and unrestricted cash transfers

description.narrative: Unconditional transfers are provided to beneficiaries without the recipient having to do anything in return in order to receive the assistance . Unrestricted transfers can be used entirely as the recipient chooses i.e. there are no restrictions on how the transfer is spent (Definitions of CALP). It can be delivered e.g. through local banks, shops, traders, local money transfer companies, remittance companies and post offices in either one or several instalments.

Appropriateness is assessed according to the SPHERE standards. A response is considered to be appropriate based on needs assessment, taking account of rights, needs, culture, age, gender, disabilities and context, and equity (non-discrimination and equal access.
